title: US Proposes Trilateral Ukraine-Russia Talks in UAE as Putin Signals Openness, While Mecca Pact Military Chiefs Activate Joint Defence and Trump Rejects Iran's 7-Day Hormuz Plan
subhead: Washington's push for face-to-face Ukraine-Russia negotiations marks a new diplomatic gear, the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence alliance moves from declaration to operational planning, and Iran's concrete Hormuz reopening proposal meets a US rejection that leaves the strait closed.

sections.heading: US Proposes First Trilateral Ukraine-Russia Meeting
sections.body:
The United States has proposed a trilateral meeting with Ukrainian and Russian representatives in the United Arab Emirates, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on September 25. The initiative, first reported by Reuters, would mark the first direct three-party negotiation format of the war if it materializes.

Russian President Vladimir Putin told India Today that all proposals remain 'on the table' and that Russia is 'open to any serious settlement process,' though he stopped short of explicitly accepting the US format. The signal marks a tonal shift from Moscow's recent position of rejecting interim arrangements.

The proposal comes amid continued Russian bombardment of Ukrainian cities. The Kyiv Post reported that Russian strikes killed seven people in Kyiv overnight, part of an escalating campaign of missile and drone attacks that has intensified through September. Ukraine has also continued its deep-strike drone campaign into Russian territory, keeping pressure on both fronts.

The UAE has emerged as the preferred venue for several reasons: its maintained relations with both Moscow and Kyiv, its role as a mediation hub throughout the conflict, and its geographic neutrality. No date has been set for the proposed meeting.
sections.whyItMatters: A trilateral format, if it occurs, would be the first time all three principal parties sit at the same table since the early 2022 Istanbul rounds. The fact that Washington is proposing it — rather than Kyiv or a neutral mediator — signals US interest in controlling the negotiation agenda.

sections.heading: Mecca Pact Military Chiefs Convene as Saudi Arabia Faces Houthi Strikes
sections.body:
Military chiefs from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey met in Riyadh on September 25 to operationalize the Mecca Defence Alliance, first signed in August. Pakistan's Army Chief General Asim Munir met with his Saudi and Turkish counterparts to finalize a joint defence mechanism, Dawn reported.

The meeting came as Saudi forces intercepted Houthi drones near Riyadh, according to Gulf News. The Houthis have expanded their strike range beyond the Red Sea corridor into central Saudi territory, raising the stakes for a defence pact that was initially framed as a mutual-security guarantee rather than an active combat alliance.

Al Arabiya reported that the alliance states plan 'urgent military talks' to support Saudi Arabia, and Turkey's parliamentary speaker suggested the pact could expand to include other Muslim-world nations, according to Reuters. Pakistan has separately stressed that the alliance is not aimed at Iran — a delicate balancing act given Pakistan's relations with Tehran.

The operationalization phase follows weeks of diplomatic groundwork. The three foreign ministers met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on September 24, and the military chiefs' meeting in Riyadh represents the shift from political declaration to military planning.
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca Pact is moving from signature to staff-level planning at a moment when Saudi Arabia is under active drone attack. If the joint defence mechanism produces deployed forces or integrated air defence, it creates a new military bloc in the Gulf — one that includes NATO member Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan, operates outside the US alliance framework, and explicitly claims to be non-adversarial toward Iran.

sections.heading: Iran's 7-Day Hormuz Plan Meets US Rejection
sections.body:
Iran formally presented a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt regional fighting, conveyed through Qatari mediators at the United Nations. Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters on Friday that 'if the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days,' according to The Star (Malaysia) and Al Jazeera.

US President Donald Trump rejected the proposal, The New Kerala reported, and is reportedly preparing military options. The rejection effectively closes the diplomatic window that opened with the June framework agreement and its short-lived ceasefire.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, during his state visit to Washington, urged both the US and Iran to return to the June framework and continue negotiations, Xinhua reported. Trump warned Xi against providing support to Iran and received assurances that China would not do so, according to the US ambassador to China. The dynamic leaves Iran without its principal diplomatic advocate at a moment when its economic lifeline — oil exports through Hormuz — remains blocked.

Oil prices slid approximately 2 percent on news of the Iranian proposal, Hindustan Times reported, reflecting market sensitivity to any de-escalation signal. European gas prices may stay elevated through winter as LNG disruptions persist, Goldman Sachs analysts told Business Today.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran has put a specific, time-bound proposal on the table and the US has rejected it. That leaves Hormuz closed, oil markets volatile, and the diplomatic track frozen — with the next move likely military rather than negotiated. China's unwillingness to back Iran, confirmed to US officials, removes Tehran's most important external lever.

sections.heading: Xi-Trump Summit Turns to Middle East as Trade Truce Holds
sections.body:
The Xi-Trump state visit concluded on September 25 with an extended trade truce but no breakthrough on fundamental disagreements. The summit's final day pivoted to the Middle East war, with both leaders discussing Iran's seven-day plan and the broader regional conflict, The Star reported.

The trade truce extension was the summit's concrete deliverable. Beyond that, the two sides appeared to manage differences rather than resolve them. Xi pressed for a return to the June Iran framework; Trump pressed for China to cut any support to Tehran. The US ambassador confirmed China gave assurances it would not support Iran — a position consistent with Beijing's interest in stable Gulf oil flows but one that constrains Tehran.

Separately, China directed a sharp warning at Japan over Taiwan on September 25. Ambassador to Japan Wu Jianghao told a reception in Tokyo that 'the Taiwan issue is the core of China's core interests, and no external interference can be tolerated,' the Seoul Daily reported. Relations between Beijing and Tokyo have cooled since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested last November that Japan could intervene in a Taiwan contingency.
sections.whyItMatters: The summit produced a holding pattern on trade and a convergence on Iran — China will not back Tehran. But Beijing's simultaneous warning to Japan over Taiwan signals that the trade truce does not extend to the security domain. The Taiwan Strait remains the fault line where Chinese pressure is intensifying, even as Washington and Beijing coordinate on the Middle East.

sections.heading: European Leaders Warn of Imminent Russian Threat
sections.body:
European leaders used the UN General Assembly's final days to issue coordinated warnings about the near-term Russian threat to the continent. ABC News (Australia) reported that the warnings came amid intelligence assessments suggesting Russia could test NATO's eastern flank within the next few years.

The declarations align with the European security debate that has intensified since Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. With US attention split between the Iran war and the Xi-Trump summit, European capitals are increasingly concerned that Washington's commitment to European defence may erode — particularly if the proposed Ukraine-Russia trilateral talks produce a settlement that freezes territorial gains.

The timing is notable: the warnings come as Switzerland prepares for its neutrality referendum on September 27. Politico reported that the vote puts Russia sanctions on the line — the initiative would enshrine stricter neutrality in the constitution, potentially barring Switzerland from adopting EU sanctions and ending peacetime NATO cooperation. Final polls show the initiative likely to fail, according to Euronews and Bloomberg, but the campaign has exposed deep domestic divisions about Switzerland's Western alignment.
sections.whyItMatters: European capitals are pre-positioning for a scenario where US security focus shifts permanently toward the Middle East and Asia. The Swiss vote, even if it fails, signals that the neutralist impulse in Europe is politically viable — and that Russia sanctions, the cornerstone of Western pressure on Moscow, remain domestically contested in at least one major European financial hub.

sections.heading: Ethiopia and Tigray: Renewed Fighting Threatens Horn of Africa Stability
sections.body:
Fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan fighters has intensified through late September, raising fears of a return to full-scale war in the Horn of Africa. France 24 reported on the renewed violence, which follows the collapse of the 2022 Pretoria agreement that ended the previous two-year conflict.

The clashes mark the most serious escalation since the ceasefire. The Horn of Africa has drawn increased international attention because of its strategic position along the Red Sea corridor — the same waterway where Houthi attacks have disrupted global shipping. Instability in Ethiopia compounds the regional security picture, affecting Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia, all of which border the conflict zone.

The African Union has called for restraint but has not deployed a mediation mission. The UN Security Council has not formally addressed the escalation, focusing instead on the Iran war and Ukraine diplomacy.
sections.whyItMatters: A second Ethiopia-Tigray war would destabilise a region already under strain from Sudan's civil war, Red Sea shipping disruptions, and great-power competition for Red Sea basing rights. The international response so far has been minimal — a gap that regional actors, including the UAE and Egypt, may fill with their own agendas.

bottomLine: Three tracks moved today. On Ukraine, Washington proposed a trilateral format that, if accepted, would bring all parties to one table for the first time in years — Putin's 'on the table' signal suggests Moscow is at least listening. On Iran, Tehran offered a concrete seven-day Hormuz reopening plan and Washington rejected it, leaving the strait closed and the diplomatic track frozen while China confirmed it will not back Iran. On the Gulf security architecture, the Mecca Pact moved from political declaration to military operational planning as Saudi Arabia absorbs Houthi drone strikes on its capital. The common thread: the US is simultaneously pushing for a Ukraine settlement, closing the Iran diplomatic window, and managing a Chinese summit — all while a new regional defence bloc takes shape outside its control.
